problem: General-purpose LLM/MLLM agents underperform specialized VLN models, and prior MLLM navigators (auxiliary modules or video tokens) are compute-heavy and inefficiently adapted. MLLMs were also unexplored for long-horizon urban VLN (Touchdown, Map2seq).
motivation: Urban VLN has much longer trajectories (up to ~55 steps) and much lower success than indoor VLN. Flamingo-style cross-attention can handle many interleaved observations without growing context length, so it may suit this setting if it is adapted to navigation with targeted synthetic data.
key_idea: Adapt a Flamingo-based MLLM into an end-to-end urban navigation agent using strided cross-attention over recent observations and a three-phase tuning scheme (street-view captioning, route summarization, then VLN fine-tuning) on GPT-synthesized data.
insight: Attending mainly to the current and most recent observations works better than attending to the full history: TC falls as stride grows, so the default stride is 1. Intermediate synthetic-data phases give consistent gains (Map2seq dev TC 53.57 -> 54.69 -> 56.95 with P1 then P2). Even without them, the architecture already beats prior SOTA (Touchdown dev TC 40.16). Baselines drop sharply under FLAME's restricted non-panoramic view (ORAR* Touchdown test TC 21.34).
method: Flamingo-based architecture: CLIP features passed through a Perceiver Resampler into N_r visual tokens per observation. Gated cross-attention injects them into the LLaMA decoder, so context length does not grow and one pass covers a whole trajectory.
Strided cross-attention: the query at step t attends only to visual tokens from the last l steps (S_t from max(0,(t-l)N_r) to t*N_r), which prioritizes recent observations; default l=1.

Action prediction: autoregressive next-action prediction over {Forward, Left, Right, Stop, Turn Around} from the instruction, observation-action history and current view; optionally a ReAct-style rationale is generated at intersections before the action.
Phase 1, single perception tuning: street-view captioning on 2,354 GPT-4V captions, trained with a language-model loss.

Phase 2, multiple perception tuning: on 4,674 synthetic simple instructions and route summaries built from an OpenStreetMap landmark graph and generated by GPT-4. The loss combines route summarization and action imitation.

Phase 3, end-to-end navigation tuning on Touchdown/Map2seq with imitation loss. It optionally adds GPT-4-synthesized rationales (6,518 Touchdown / 6,291 Map2seq trajectories), evaluated with GPT-4-judged RC and RA metrics and self-consistency voting.

setting.training_data: Touchdown (9,326 pairs) and Map2seq (7,672 pairs) plus synthetic data: 2,354 GPT-4V street-view captions, 4,674 GPT-4 route summaries/simple instructions, and GPT-4 rationales (6,518 Touchdown / 6,291 Map2seq)
setting.observation: monocular RGB street-view crops (limited field of view, not panoramic), history of observations and actions
setting.action_space: discrete: Forward, Left, Right, Stop, Turn Around on the StreetLearn nav graph
setting.privileged: none (synthetic route summaries use OpenStreetMap landmark data at training time only)

numbers.extra: synthetic captions and summaries for phases 1-2; single A100, 14h training

numbers.eval_set_note: Dev set; ablation without phases 1 and 2

numbers_note: Touchdown and Map2seq are reported by the paper's Dev/Test sets; 'val' is used for Dev. Reasoning results (RC/RA) on subsets are in Table 2 and not listed. The stride ablation appears only as a figure.
results: FLAME sets a new SOTA on Touchdown test with TC 40.20, beating Loc4Plan (32.90) by 7.3 points, and on Map2seq test with TC 52.44, beating VELMA (48.70) by 3.74 points. It stays strong with restricted non-panoramic views, where the re-implemented baselines degrade sharply.
limitations: Evaluated only on the two StreetLearn-based urban datasets (Touchdown, Map2seq), with no indoor or continuous-environment evaluation.
Depends on GPT-4/GPT-4V synthetic data and a GPT-4-based evaluator whose raw scores needed calibration against humans (50 instances).
Uses discrete nav-graph actions with cropped views, so real-world applicability is untested.
